
```{r}
lit_clean <- lit |>

lit_clean
```

```{r}
# import life expectancy
health <- WDI(country = "all",
  indicator = "SP.DYN.LE00.IN",  # Life Expectancy in (years)
  latest = 1 #returns most recent non-empty value
)
```

```{r}
# import land area
area <- WDI(country = "all",
  indicator = "AG.LND.TOTL.K2",  # Land Area (sq.km)
  latest = 1 #returns most recent non-empty value
)
```

```{r}
# import gdp per capita
wealth <- WDI(country = "all",
  indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.CD",  # GDP per cap (ppp)
  latest = 1 #returns most recent non-empty value
)
```


```{r}
# find row index of Afghanistan
health_start <- which(health$country == "Afghanistan")
area_start <- which(area$country == "Afghanistan")
wealth_start <- which(wealth$country == "Afghanistan")
```


```{r}
health_clean <- health |>
  slice(health_start:n()) |>  # keep countries only (not aggregates)
  select(country, country_code = iso3c, year_health = year, life_exp = SP.DYN.LE00.IN)
health_clean
```



```{r}
area_clean <- area |>
  slice(area_start:n()) |>  # keep countries only (not aggregates)
  select(country, country_code = iso3c, year_area = year, land_area = AG.LND.TOTL.K2)
area_clean
```



```{r}
wealth_clean <- wealth |>
  slice(wealth_start:n()) |>  # keep countries only (not aggregates)
  select(country, country_code = iso3c, year_wealth = year, gdp_per_cap = NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.CD)
wealth_clean
```


```{r}
# merge data frames
country <- merge(lit_clean, merge(health_clean, merge(area_clean, wealth_clean)))
head(country)
```

```{r}
country <- country |>
  select(country, gdp_per_cap, lit_rate, life_exp, land_area)
head(country)
```

# Exploring Relations


The covariance is one statistic we can use to measure the relation between two variables:

$$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E \big[ (X - \mu_x)(Y - \mu_y) \big]$$

The Pearson correlation coefficient is a normalized measure of the linear association between two variables that results in a value between $-1$ and $1$.

$$\rho_{X,Y} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_x \sigma_y}$$

When working with sample data, we denote the correlation coefficient with $r$, and we can interpret the value as follows:

- If $r$ is close to zero, then there not a strong linear association between the two variables.
- If $r$ is positive, there is a positive linear association between the variables.
- If $r$ is negative, there is a negative linear association between the variables.
- The closer the $|r|$ is to $1$, the stronger the linear relationship.
- Two variables can very strongly related and have $r \approx 0$ if the relation is not linear.

![Image with Different Correlation Values](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Correlation_examples2.svg/500px-Correlation_examples2.svg.png)



```{r}
cor(country[-1])  # exclude column 1
```


```{r}
pairs(country[-1])
```

```{r}
country_log
```


```{r}
pairs(country_log[-1])  # exclude column 1
```


## Comparing Models

---

```{r}
wealth_lmod <- lm(gdp_per_cap ~ lit_rate, country)
summary(wealth_lmod)
```

```{r}
plot(gdp_per_cap ~ lit_rate, data = country,
     pch = 20,
#     col=ifelse(literacy_rate > 94.50318 & literacy_rate < 94.5032, "red", "sea green"),
     main = "Scatterplot of Education vs Wealth",
     xlab = "Literacy Rate (%)",

abline(wealth_lmod, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}

```



# Simple Linear Regression

The [**simple linear regression**]{style="color:blue"} is a linear regression model with a single predictor $X$ and a single response variable $Y$. It does not refer to the complexity of the linear model. The most common simple linear regression model is the familiar

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon .$$



## Error Assumptions

---

A simple linear regression model of the form $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon$ has the following key assumptions about the errors of prediction: 

- [**Linearity**]{style="color:blue"}: $Y$ and $X$ have a linear relationship. In other words, the mean value of $Y$ is a straight-line function of $X$. If the have a nonlinear association, we should modify our model or transform predictor and/or response variables.

$$E(Y | X=x_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$$


- [**Mean Zero**]{style="color:blue"}: We do not want our model to be biased.

$$E(\epsilon_i) = E(\epsilon | X=x_i) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } x_i.$$

- [**The Errors are Uncorrelated**]{style="color:blue"}: The error in one prediction does not effect the amount of error in any other prediction.

$$\text{Cov}(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j ) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } i \ne j .$$ 

- [**Homoscedasticity**]{style="color:blue"}: The model is equally accurate everywhere. Thus, the errors of prediction have the same, constant variance. We do not want the model to be more accurate when $x$ is small and less accurate when $x$ is large.

$$\text{Var}(\epsilon_i) = \text{Var}(\epsilon | X = x_i) = \sigma^2 \qquad \text{for all } x_i .$$

- [**Normality**]{style="color:blue"}: The errors are normally distributed. Most observations of $Y_i$ are close to the prediction $\hat{Y}_i$, and we are less and less likely to observe values $Y_i$ farther and farther away from the prediction.


We can summarize several of the assumptions on $\epsilon_i$ as follows. For all $\epsilon_i$, we have

$$\large \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{Cov}(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j) = 0 \ \ \text{ if } i \ne j.$$
